summary: Describes Path Computation Element Communication Protocol extensions for the auto-bandwidth feature, which automatically adjusts the bandwidth reserved for an MPLS-TE path based on the traffic flowing through it, when a stateful PCE controls the paths.

plainLanguage.summary: A pipe can widen or narrow depending on how much water flows. This lets a central planner do that automatically for network paths.

questions: how does mpls te auto bandwidth work
what is the pcep auto-bandwidth capability tlv
subtitle: How a router and a path computation server agree on automatically resizing the bandwidth reserved for a traffic-engineered path.

tldr.problem: Traffic on an MPLS-TE path changes over time, so a fixed bandwidth reservation is either wasted or too small. When a stateful PCE controls the path, PCEP has no way to carry the auto-bandwidth settings or the resulting adjustments.
tldr.mechanism: The head-end router (the PCC) samples the traffic, works out the new bandwidth to reserve, and reports it to the PCE. A new capability TLV and an attributes TLV with sub-TLVs carry the tuning knobs, and a notification lets either side ask the other to pause.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9756. It gives PCC-initiated and PCE-initiated LSPs a common way to use auto-bandwidth under an active stateful PCE.

today: RFC 8733 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9756, so read the two together. The text of this RFC does not say how widely the extensions are deployed.

sections.title: Auto-Bandwidth with a Stateful PCE
sections.content:
PCEP lets a Path Computation Client (PCC) and a Path Computation Element (PCE) cooperate on MPLS-TE Label Switched Paths (LSPs). RFC 8231 adds stateful control, and RFC 8281 lets a PCE create LSPs. RFC 8733 focuses on the active stateful PCE, where the PCE controls the LSPs.

An LSP set up with some bandwidth may need a different reservation as traffic changes. The head-end router watches the real demand and periodically computes a new bandwidth. This feature is commonly called auto-bandwidth. In this document the PCC, which is the head-end of the LSP, collects the samples and calculates the Adjusted Bandwidth, then reports it to the PCE.

Sending the raw measured values to the PCE instead, and having the PCE calculate the adjustment, are both out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A water pipe should be as wide as the water that flows through it. The router measures the flow and tells the planner how wide the pipe needs to be.

sections.title: How Auto-Bandwidth Works
sections.content:
If the traffic on an LSP is lower than its reservation, the extra bandwidth is wasted. If it is higher, it can cause congestion or packet loss. The initial bandwidth can be any value, including zero. Adjustments must not disrupt traffic, and make-before-break signaling is one way to achieve that.

The PCC takes a Bandwidth-Sample of the traffic rate at every Sample-Interval, with a default of 5 minutes. Samples pile up over an Adjustment-Interval, with a default of 24 hours. The highest sample is the MaxAvgBw. The LSP is resized to it only if it differs from the current reservation by at least the threshold, which can be an absolute value or a percentage, with a default of 5 percent.

A long interval hides sudden changes, so overflow and underflow thresholds can force an early adjustment when a sudden rise or fall persists for a set number of consecutive samples. These have no defaults. A Minimum-Threshold stops a percentage rule from triggering constant resignaling at very low bandwidth values.

Any bandwidth change means resignaling the LSP, which can preempt lower-priority LSPs. At scale this causes signaling churn, so operators are advised to choose parameters to suit the number of LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: Every few minutes the router checks how much water went through. At the end of the day it picks the busiest reading and widens or narrows the pipe, but only if the change is big enough to matter.

sections.title: Capability Advertisement
sections.content:
During PCEP initialization, a speaker includes the AUTO-BANDWIDTH-CAPABILITY TLV in its OPEN object to say it supports these extensions. It has Type 36 and a fixed Length of 4 octets, and its single 32-bit Flag field has no defined flags. Unassigned bits MUST be sent as 0 and ignored on receipt.

The extensions MUST NOT be used unless both speakers included the TLV. A speaker that does not know the extension just ignores the TLV, as RFC 5440 requires. If a speaker supports the extensions but did not advertise the capability and then receives an auto-bandwidth attributes TLV, it SHOULD send a PCErr with Error-Type 19 and Error-value 14, and ignore that TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: Before they use the new trick, both sides hold up a card saying they know it. If only one has a card, they do not use it.

sections.title: The Attributes TLV and Its Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The AUTO-BANDWIDTH-ATTRIBUTES TLV (Type 37) is an optional TLV in the LSPA object. It carries the configurable knobs as sub-TLVs. It is present in all PCEP messages for the LSP while the feature is enabled, and its absence means the speaker wants the feature off. Sub-TLVs are included when they have changed since the last message, and defaults apply for any missing ones in the first message.

All sub-TLVs are optional. Unrecognized ones MUST be ignored, and if a type appears more than once only the first is processed. An invalid value makes the sub-TLV ignored and the previous value is kept.

  • Intervals: the Sample-Interval and Adjustment-Interval range from 1 to 604800 seconds (7 days). The defaults are 300 and 86400 seconds. The Sample-Interval MUST NOT be greater than the Adjustment-Interval. A Down-Adjustment-Interval can override the interval for downward trends.
  • Thresholds: absolute thresholds are IEEE floating point values in bytes per second. Percentage thresholds are integers from 1 to 100, with 0 invalid, and carry a Minimum-Threshold. If both forms are given, either one can trigger an adjustment.
  • Limits: Minimum-Bandwidth and Maximum-Bandwidth bound what auto-bandwidth may reserve.
  • Overflow and underflow: these carry a 5-bit Count of consecutive samples, where 0 is invalid. The Overflow-Threshold needs to be at least the Up-Adjustment-Threshold, and likewise for underflow and the Down-Adjustment-Threshold.
sections.plainLanguage: The settings are like a recipe card: how often to measure, how big a change counts, and the smallest and biggest the pipe may get.

sections.title: Messages and the BANDWIDTH Object
sections.content:
For a PCE-initiated LSP with the feature on, the attributes TLV MUST be in the LSPA object of the PCInitiate message. The PCE can also send it in PCUpd messages to change parameters. For delegated PCC-initiated LSPs it is carried in PCRpt. The PCEP message formats themselves are unchanged.

The PCC reports the calculated bandwidth (MaxAvgBw) in the existing BANDWIDTH object with Object-Type 1, Requested Bandwidth. The reoptimization bandwidth (Object-Type 2) is not needed, since the stateful PCE already knows the LSP's bandwidth. For PCE-initiated LSPs, the PCC creates the LSP from the PCE's attributes, then delegates it back to the PCE automatically and sends a PCRpt.

If either side is swamped, it SHOULD send a PCNtf with Notification-type 5 (Auto-Bandwidth Overwhelm State) and Notification-value 1. The peer SHOULD then stop sending auto-bandwidth messages, and MUST ignore any that arrive. An optional OVERLOADED-DURATION TLV gives the pause length. Value 2 clears the state. Dampening is RECOMMENDED to avoid oscillation.
sections.plainLanguage: The router tells the planner the new pipe size it wants. If either one is too busy, it shouts "slow down" and the other waits until it says it is ready again.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Auto-bandwidth SHOULD be controllable per LSP, and the parameters SHOULD be configurable by an operator. Maximum-Bandwidth and Minimum-Bandwidth should be set to limits that do not harm the rest of the MPLS-TE domain.

Each enabled LSP adds load: the PCC monitors and reports, the PCE recomputes, and the PCC resignals. An implementation SHOULD allow a limit on how many LSPs use the feature, and MAY allow a limit on the rate of related messages. A Sample-Interval much shorter than the 5-minute default, such as 1 minute or less, could interact badly with transport protocols because they have too little time to settle after one adjustment before the next samples are taken. If an invalid sub-TLV value is ignored, the implementation SHOULD log it.
sections.plainLanguage: Resizing pipes takes work for everyone, so do not turn it on for too many pipes, and do not measure too often.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The new TLVs add no substantial security concerns beyond those in RFC 8231 and RFC 8281. It is RECOMMENDED that the extensions only be activated on authenticated and encrypted sessions between PCEs and PCCs in the same administrative authority, using TLS as described in RFC 8253.

Incorrect auto-bandwidth parameters could harm the LSP and the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Only let trusted friends change the pipe settings, over a locked line, because wrong settings can cause trouble.

viz.caption: SUB-TLV TYPES OF THE ATTRIBUTES TLV (RFC 8733)

items.label: Adjustment-Interval
items.desc: How often to adjust, up and down.

items.label: Down-Adjustment-Interval
items.desc: Overrides the interval for downward trends.

items.label: Adjustment-Threshold
items.desc: Absolute difference that triggers a change.

items.label: Adjustment-Threshold-Percentage
items.desc: Percentage difference that triggers a change.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Fixed length of the value in octets.

fields.name: Flag
fields.desc: No flags are defined; reserved bits are sent as 0.
